findings.statement: NF-kB pathway activity is raised in inflamed or UC mucosa in all eight cohorts, with the strongest signal in GSE206285 (t [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=18.79]); TNFa is likewise up in all eight cohorts, which fits the TNF axis that is already drug-targeted.

JAK-STAT pathway activity is up in all eight cohorts with no cohort going down, supporting the already-drugged JAK inhibitor class. Broad activation, shared with NFkB, TNFa, MAPK, PI3K, TGFb, EGFR and hypoxia, so it does not discriminate between candidates.

Inferred STAT3 TF activity is up in all eight cohorts, peaking in GSE206285 (t [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=24.0]). It is inferred from target genes, not from STAT3 mRNA; AP1 is also up in all eight cohorts, so the TF layer is dominated by generic inflammatory and stress programmes.

Not every pathway rises: p53 is down in a minority of cohorts and up in none, so p53 does not support an inflamed-mucosa activation signature. Androgen is inconsistent in direction across cohorts, and Trail, VEGF and Estrogen rise in only some cohorts.

CXCL8 is the top-ranked secreted neutrophil-attracting ligand, up in all eight cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.864]). Its transcripts come mainly from macrophages in Smillie data, but when neutrophils are included they hold most of the transcript share (Neutrophil CXCR4, Neutrophil and Neutrophil OSM lead), and a second dataset agrees on a myeloid source.

CXCR2 ranks first in the convergence ranking, with genetics, literature and tractability support and phase 2 and phase 3 antagonists (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682). Single-cell data place its transcripts almost entirely in neutrophils (share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), so the bulk signal reflects neutrophil infiltration rather than a change of epithelium or stroma. It is not yet an approved UC target.

CXCL8-CXCR2 is a neutrophil-to-neutrophil autocrine/paracrine circuit: Neutrophil CXCR4 sends CXCL8 to the generic Neutrophil state with log2 change vs uninflamed [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.755]. Other CXCR2 pairs involve Neutrophil OSM and Neutrophil PADI4 as receivers. This is co-expression only, not proof of signalling.

CXCL8 also reaches ACKR1 endothelial cells, with the largest rise from the generic Neutrophil sender (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.991]). ACKR1 is an atypical chemokine receptor, so this is a venular presentation or leukocyte-trafficking circuit, not classical signalling. Only anti-IL-8 antibodies (ABX-IL-8, phase 2) target the ligand.

CXCR1 is the rank-two candidate and replicates in most cohorts but not all (meta log2FC [gene=CXCR1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.662]). It shares the dual CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists with CXCR2, so the two are one druggable axis, still unapproved in UC.

IL1B is up in all eight cohorts and is sent mainly by monocyte-derived macrophages to neutrophil states through IL1R2, which is mostly a decoy receptor (log2 change to Neutrophil PADI4 [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.168]). So the top IL1B pairs may not represent activating signalling. Canakinumab is approved for other diseases, not UC.

TREM1 is a myeloid receptor up in all eight cohorts, with only the phase 2 peptide nangibotide as a drug, so it is an under-explored neutrophil/monocyte target in UC. It has no genetic support in the ranking.

IDO1 is up in all eight cohorts with strong literature but no genetic evidence; IDO1 inhibitors exist, but they come from oncology and their direction in UC is unclear, since IDO1 is probably an interferon-induced counter-regulatory gene.

MMP1, MMP3, MMP7 and MMP10 are among the top replicated up-regulated genes (all eight cohorts) and are the stromal-remodelling arm. Broad MMP inhibitors (marimastat) failed historically for toxicity and specificity reasons, so this remains largely untargeted.

caveats: PROGENy and CollecTRI activities are inferred from bulk biopsies; inflamed mucosa activates nearly every pathway at once, partly through immune-cell infiltration, so broad pathway rank is non-specific.
Ligand-receptor scores are co-expression of mean CP10K, not evidence of signalling, and are from one single-cell dataset (Gubatan 2026).
Neutrophils are absent from Smillie, so CXCR2 and CXCL8 cell attribution differs between the datasets; CXCR2 was not replicated in the second dataset.
No fibroblast-targeting neutrophil cytokine circuit (for example OSM to inflammatory fibroblasts) was tested here, so no claim is made about it.
Top convergence ranks are dominated by neutrophil chemokine and mucosal-injury genes; the ranking does not itself establish causality.
The anti-TNF, anti-IL-23, integrin and JAK classes were not independently checked beyond pathway activity.
